subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Supercar Wars
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Supercar Wars.

hook.text: In the 1980s, supercars stopped being fast road cars and became engineering weapons.

buildup.text: The Ferrari F40, Porsche 959, and Lamborghini Countach all pushed past 180 mph.

discovery.text: Then McLaren's F1 in 1992 hit 240 mph using a gold-lined engine bay and a central driver's seat.

twist.text: Each new record lasted shorter. Bugatti, Koenigsegg, and Hennessey kept one-upping each other.

climax.text: Today, hypercars exceed 300 mph—speeds that make 1980s supercars look almost ordinary.

punchline.text: The supercar war has no finish line.

details.summary: The supercar wars of the 1980s through 2000s saw Ferrari, Lamborghini, Porsche, and McLaren compete to build the fastest and most exclusive road cars, pushing automotive technology to extremes.
details.whyItMatters: Supercar competition drove innovations in aerodynamics, carbon fiber, turbocharging, and active suspension that eventually trickled down to everyday production vehicles.
takeaways: The McLaren F1 held the speed record from 1998 to 2005
The Bugatti Veyron broke the 250 mph barrier in 2005
Carbon fiber and active aero became standard in the segment

faq.question: What's the difference between a supercar and a hypercar?
faq.answer: There are no official definitions, but hypercars are generally considered the absolute top tier, with over 1,000 horsepower, seven-figure prices, and extremely limited production numbers.

faq.question: Do supercars serve any purpose beyond showing off?
faq.answer: They serve as technology laboratories. Innovations tested in supercars, such as carbon fiber bodies, turbo hybridization, and active aerodynamics, frequently appear in mainstream models within a decade.
